"The Graduate Admissions Committee in the Department of English at the University of Florida has completed its review of applications and, unfortunately, has not selected you for admission.
 
This is no reflection on your academic excellence. We received more than 200 applications from talented and accomplished students all over the world for our graduate program, and we have admitted fewer than 10%. With so many excellent applicants to choose from, our decisions often came down to judgments about which students we can best support with our particular faculty expertise, our library resources, and the teaching and other training opportunities we can provide. Many of those who applied to our program can, we believe, actually be served better elsewhere. We hope that you get that opportunity, and we wish you luck and success in your future endeavors.
 
One final note: because we had so many applicants, we are unable to offer each applicant a detailed response on our Admissions Committee’s decision. Thank you for considering the University of Florida and for giving us an opportunity to review your materials. We are always amazed and humbled by the astonishing work that applicants to our program intend to do in the future. This year is no exception."

After charging over $100 for an application fee, this sort of treatment stings. I understand funding cuts and online application platform errors; however, as an institution, when you charge that much to apply, you need to have the integrity to treat each applicant with respect for the work they have done. It's great that the university received 210 applicants, but it's not an awesome feeling to be treated as a system error that slipped through the cracks. All this being said, I have already accepted another offer. I just wanted the peace of mind.

comments: Interviewed 2.10 and genuinely thought it went well. Proposed research: 19th- 20th-century American poetry; my writing sample brought existentialist thought - especially the work of Jean-Paul Sartre - into discourse with American poetics. All the indicators looks good. Then... no waitlist, no unofficial offer... I understand since before the decision came out that I had made the finalist pool but not the admit pool or waitlist (about 2 people were admitted from what I've heard; yet, if you look at the website, about 10-15 professors are seeking advisees... meaning only 2 professors, probably very distinguished, had the negotiating power to have their pick... the person I chose as a potential advisor probably didn't have the bandwidth or the care for philosophical approaches that my dissertation gestured toward...). I know now how to position myself for next cycle (I only applied to one English program this cycle, Harvard's); next time I'll be applying to all 8 Ivy English PhDs and will write dissertations that draw from the work of more senior level professors to ensure I get in.... just putting this all here because it really is a journey, and nobody was there to advise me exactly on how to go about it :)

The number of admission offers available at Princeton for entering graduate students is extremely limited, and we cannot offer admission to all applicants who are well qualified. Indeed, many departments have applicants who could be admitted if it were possible to accommodate additional students. Our decisions take into account not only the applicants’ merits but also the suitability of the programs to the candidates’ expressed interests. Our goal is to achieve a sound match between the strengths of our programs and the interests of the relatively small number of outstanding students that can be accommodated.

Unfortunately, due to the volume of applications which we receive, it is not possible for the department or the Graduate School to go back and review applications to justify the denial or offer advice on fortifying a future application.

comments: I presume it's a rejection, anyway, because surely "hmm we're struggling to figure out how to make the system display the details ... check tomorrow" is not what they'd choose for acceptances and waitlists.  I feel for the person I'm in email contact with, who sounds unsupported in their job (which perhaps also happened in 2024 if you look back in these results?).  I emailed asking when I might get my decision because it seems late.  They emailed back very promptly saying it should be in the portal.  I responded that when I log in to ApplyWeb, on the page where I can see all the universities that used ApplyWeb, there is a "decision letter" button above the "checklist" button but this doesn't appear for Cornell.  They responded that perhaps it needs to process overnight, but let them know if I still didn't see it tomorrow.  I talked to the tech support bot which suggests (Interesting to know!) that universities load a bunch of decision letters and then have to add a date and time and give permission for the student to view it (so if the college says it's there and I say it's not, they probably didn't give permission yet).  I sent that info to the kind administrative person at Cornell's History Graduate program, who thanked me for it and said it gave them an idea of a few things to go check.  Sounds like the funding cuts really hit a lot of areas -- my home department has had a lot of cuts and it's our admin person who is bearing the brunt of a lot of it.  Anyway.  Still can't see a decision in the portal, but it's apparent my application is just an administrative loose end, and this cycle has taught me that my research niche is "weird" and difficult for programs to find space for.  1a/7r/3p is I think the current tally, one pending is a Public Policy program.

comments:
I reached out to UConn because I had not heard. Only then did I get a rejection email, which essentially told me that even though I was not being considered, I wouldn't receive a rejection until after April 15th. Idk if this is a common occurrence, but I find it to be a bit disrespectful either way, after all the time we spend on these apps. The email I was sent is below:

"Thank you for your email and continued interest in UConn’s MA program. At this time, we have issued offers of acceptance to a very small number of applicants, as well as notifications to a few others that they have been placed on a selective waitlist. It is unlikely that we will move beyond our waitlist this year. Official decisions for all remaining applicants will likely be released after the April 15th deadline, as UConn adheres to the Council of Graduate Schools’ (CGS) “April 15 Resolution”: April 15 Resolution - CGS (cgsnet.org). Applicants who have received offers have until April 15th to respond."

Thank you for the time, effort, and passion you put into your application to the UCSC Physics graduate program. There is a person behind every application, statement of purpose, and letter of recommendation, and we truly appreciate the effort you contributed applying to our program. That is what makes it challenging to inform you we are unable to recommend you for admission for this coming fall.

This was a difficult decision for our committee for two reasons: 1) this year’s applicant pool was exceptionally talented, and the level of research experience and academic dedication we saw was genuinely humbling; and 2) due to department funding and faculty research capacity we are simply unable to recommend offers of admission to all researchers we believe would thrive here.

This decision is a reflection of our departmental constraints, not a reflection of your potential as a physicist. There are many paths towards scientific inquiry, and we hope you continue pursuing your interests in physics research.

Understandably, many applicants ask us for feedback on their applications to see how they can improve in the future. Please understand due to the sheer number of requests we receive the committee is unable to provide comment on any individual's application. We trust that your continued efforts and dedication will open doors for you as you pursue your career.

Thank you again for considering UC Santa Cruz. We wish you the very best in your next chapter.

The Admissions Committee has now completed its review of the applications for Fall 2026. I regret to inform you that you have not been admitted into the program.

When making admissions decisions we consider the applicant's academic record, type and range of teaching and professional experiences, and specified research interests. In addition to selecting only those applicants with top ratings in all of these categories, we look for those whose research interests closely match the scholarly expertise of the APLNG faculty. Thus, each year we reject applicants with strong applications but with research interests that are not the best fit with our faculty.  This year, the decisions were particularly difficult as we had a large number of highly qualified applicants.

I regret that our decision could not be more positive. On behalf of the Admissions Committee, I wish you continued success in your academic and professional endeavors.

Email from DGS. Honestly thought the interview went well, and it was my top choice, which makes it even harder. That said, I have to give them credit: it's probably the kindest and most considerate rejection letter I've ever received, acknowledging the time and effort applicants put in. Still sad, but grateful for the thoughtful note.

"...Applying to graduate school takes significant energy and time, and we were honored that you included us among your choices for application. While we aren’t able to offer specific feedback on your application, please know that our decision this year is not a negative evaluation of your suitability for graduate school or a career in the history profession. Each year, we must forego the opportunity to work with and learn from many talented applicants. The loss is entirely ours, and we hope that you will find another path where you will be supported to pursue your passions."
